title: Kantian Epistemology, Hegelian Dialectics, and the Unity of Science: The Heuristic of Totality and the Ouroboros Principle
content: This article develops a systematic model for reconnecting transcendental philosophy, dialectical method, and contemporary philosophy of science. Its central thesis is that Kantian epistemology remains indispensable because knowledge is mediated by the conditions of possible experience, but that those conditions cannot be treated as ahistorical or immaterial. Through Hegelian Aufhebung, the transcendental subject is reinterpreted as a material, biocultural, neurodynamic, and historically formed dialectical subject. The Heuristic of Totality names the methodological operation required by this transformation: the disciplined integration of partial knowledges across physics, biology, neuroscience, anthropology, history, and critical philosophy without reducing one domain to another. The Ouroboros Principle extends this method into a recursive theory of science, in which scientific inquiry studies the brain, organism, culture, institutions, and symbolic systems that make scientific inquiry possible. The argument develops the Phenomenon/Noumenon distinction as a mobile frontier of intelligibility; defends a Cosmopoietic conception of immanent creation; rejects dualism and transcendence; and articulates an emergentist physicalism capable of linking consciousness, information, embodiment, and culture. Against positivist demarcation and postmodern fragmentation, the article proposes a post-positivist realism in which truth is materially constrained, historically situated, and recursively self-corrective. It also clarifies the philosophical path from Kant and Hegel to Spinozist immanence, showing why later theories of neurodynamic consciousness, mass-energy-consciousness equivalence, and computerized neuropsychological assessment should be read as developments of a prior monist and anti-dualist architecture. The result is a dense framework for the unity of science, consciousness studies, and continental philosophy under a single dialectical and cosmopoietic research program.
